title: Vayikra: when a leader errs (Leviticus 4:22)
hookLine: the text says "when", not "if"; leaders will make mistakes
tomorrow: Tzav: the fire shall not go out

cards: When did you last hear a leader admit a mistake in public? A boss, a principal, a mayor, a coach. Not a vague we regret any confusion, but a plain I got that wrong.

It's rare enough that people remember it. Chapter four of Leviticus lists offerings for mistakes made without meaning to. It goes through four kinds of people, from the high priest down to an ordinary individual.
Three are introduced with the word if. One gets a different word. He's the leader.

teach.h: IF, IF, IF, AND THEN: WHEN.
teach.b: Here's the list. If the anointed priest sins. If the whole congregation errs.
If any one of the common people sins. And in between: "When a ruler sinneth." The Hebrew there is asher, when, instead of im, if.
The ruler, the nasi, is a tribal chief or a king, someone with real power.

These are errors made without intent; the Hebrew calls it shegagah, an honest slip. And for a person in charge, the text seems to assume they will happen. Commentators heard two things in that small word.
Some read it as a warning: power makes mistakes almost certain. The more decisions you make, and the more people you affect, the more often you'll be wrong. Rashi hears something hopeful.
He cites the Talmud, which plays on the sound of asher and hears ashrei, happy. Happy is the generation whose leader brings an offering for his mistakes.
If he admits the ones he made without meaning to, how much more will he regret the ones he made on purpose.

So the leader isn't excused, and he isn't condemned for being human. He's expected to own it, publicly, by walking up to the altar with everyone watching. A leader who never errs isn't in the Torah's picture at all.
A leader who admits it is a gift to the whole generation.

how: Jewish teaching often cites the Talmud's 'happy is the generation whose leader brings an offering for his mistakes' when speaking about leaders acknowledging error.

o: an honest slip: a mistake made unaware
a ruler: a chief or king of a tribe
and He called: this portion's first word

games.q: what's inside the chapter — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah says 'if a ruler sins'
it says when: asher, not im.
Leviticus 4 is about mistakes made without intent
the Talmud hears ashrei, happy, in the word for when
happy is the generation whose leader brings an offering for his mistakes.

games.q: you're a tribal chief, and you've realized you broke a law without meaning to. the whole camp will see if you bring an offering. what does the Torah expect?
o: keep quiet: a leader can't look weak.
bring the offering and own the mistake.
have someone else bring it for you.
games.why: he brings his own offering. and the Talmud says: happy is the generation whose leader does that.

practice: Think of someone with responsibility over you, at work, at school, at home or in your community, who got something wrong without meaning to, and notice what you still carry about it.
Try seeing it the Torah's way: of course they slipped; they lead. And if you're in charge somewhere, bring to mind one slip of your own you could name plainly.

wordCard.voice: Vayikra. And He called. The book that says when a ruler errs, not if, and asks the leader to own it in public.

orig.note: Hebrew: when a ruler sins, Leviticus 4:22.

carryVoice: Your line: when, not if. Owning a slip is part of leading. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Rashi on Leviticus 4:22; Babylonian Talmud, Horayot 10b
